title: Short Stuff: Chinatowns
summary: Short Stuff episode on Chinatowns in the United States. Josh and Chuck trace why Chinese immigrant enclaves formed, from the 1850s influx drawn by railroads, gold rush and lumber work, through the first Chinatown in San Francisco (then called Little Canton), the 1875 Page Law's effect on women in Chinatown, and the tongs and district associations that housed and employed newcomers. They then cover the turn to xenophobia and violence, including the 1871 Los Angeles lynching, the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act, and anti-Chinese attacks during the plague scare. The episode closes with post-WWII easing of restrictions, the roughly fifty Chinatowns today, Buford Highway in Atlanta, suburban Chinatowns such as Monterey Park, and gentrification pressures.
topics: Chinese immigration to the United States
Chinese immigrant women and family reunification

segments.title: Opening banter and why Chinatowns formed
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic and his interest in ethnic enclaves. He explains that Chinatowns began as a refuge from racial exclusion, and that Chinese immigrants arrived in large numbers in the 1850s drawn by railroad work, the California gold rush, and lumber mills in the Pacific Northwest.
topics: Chinese immigration to the United States

segments.title: Early San Francisco Chinatown and demographics
segments.summary: The hosts describe the first formally recognized Chinatown in San Francisco, called Little Canton in the 1850s after the Canton region. They note the 1853 newspaper use of the word Chinatown, a twelve-block area with about 22,000 residents by the late 1880s, and a ratio of roughly twenty men to every woman due to the Page Law of 1875. Women began arriving more after World War Two, making Chinatowns more family oriented.

segments.title: Community institutions: pai fang, tongs and district associations
segments.summary: The hosts describe the pai fang decorated gateway arches and the businesses Chinatowns were known for, such as shoemaking, laundry, and cigar production. They explain the social, district and family organizations, and the tongs, which provided housing, jobs and legal help to newly arrived immigrants.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a short break before moving to the discussion of anti-Chinese hostility.

segments.title: Xenophobia and violence against Chinatowns
segments.summary: The hosts describe the shift from tolerance to xenophobia, with Chinatowns becoming targets for white mobs in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. They cite an 1871 Los Angeles mob that lynched seventeen Chinese men and boys, and say Governor John Bigler called for more restrictions. Anti-Chinese journalism portrayed Chinatowns as dirty and crime-ridden, and Chinatowns in Honolulu and San Francisco were affected during the bubonic plague scare.

segments.title: Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882
segments.summary: The hosts explain the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, one of America's first restrictive immigration laws. It barred new Chinese immigration and prevented those already in the country from becoming naturalized citizens. Restrictions remained tight for about sixty years until World War Two began to relax them.

segments.title: Modern Chinatowns, Atlanta's Buford Highway and suburban shift
segments.summary: The hosts say there are roughly fifty Chinatowns in the US today. Atlanta lacks a traditional Chinatown but has Buford Highway, a multi-ethnic corridor. They list other Chinatowns, note that Monterey Park, California, was dubbed the first suburban Chinatown and became majority Asian American in the 1990s, and discuss gentrification pushing residents out and efforts to preserve cultural character.
topics: Chinatowns in the United States today

segments.title: Closing thoughts and travel tip
segments.summary: The hosts note San Francisco's Chinatown remains the most vibrant, while Washington DC's Chinatown has few Chinese residents now. Chuck gives a travel tip to bring cash for dim sum places, and the episode closes with the show credits.
